title: I built it, It's free,  And All I ask for is your feedback
author: malsi_
selftext:
Hey  I built BenAwf (a Strategy Lab for Algo trading). It’s free to use (MCP or bring your own model key). **I’m not selling anything here**; I want honest feedback from people who actually backtest.

What I cared about most was not lying to myself with a pretty equity curve.

A few things under the hood (rules backtests):

**1-minute clock** The backtest steps on a 1-minute bar clock — same 1-minute cadence as live entry-rule checks.

**Exits aren’t close-only** Between steps we walk those 1-minute bars and test stop/target against each bar’s low → high → close path (open-high-low-close path inside the bar — not a full tick tape).

**No peeking ahead on indicators** At each sim time we only use bars at or before that time, and rule values resolve on the latest closed bar for that chart timeframe. Live and backtest share the same rules evaluator.

**Costs (honest limitation)** We use a standard 0.1% fee model. We do **not** account for slippage yet — so treat fills as cleaner than a busy live market.

**Paper first** Paper trading is ready to use. Connecting a live venue is still beta.

If you build or backtest strategies: try it, break it, tell me what’s missing or what smells wrong.

Link: [https://benawf.com](https://benawf.com/)

The demo below is the most impressive backtest so far

Thanks.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the low to high to close walk inside the bar is the bit most 1-minute backtesters skip, so good on you for writing it down. one thing that smells: when the stop and the target both sit inside the same bar, that ordering always fills the stop first for longs, so trend bars get punished and reversal bars get flattered. worth logging how often both land in one bar, if it is rare it does not matter.

I built Quantradin, which is in the same corner as you, paper only and free, so take this as one builder to another: the thing I would push on before slippage is the spread on the fill. a flat 0.1% looks fine on SPY and quietly flatters anything thin. a spread taken from the quote at fill time changed more for me than the path model ever did.

replies.author: malsi_
replies.body:
knowing how often both land in one bar requires granular bars, which is tecnicly challenging if you want to offer a generous backtest window to users, populair platform offer 5000 bars of free subs and some don't go beyond 3000 on payed ones 

we do 300.000 ! 

my approach to handle this is: go pesemistic ( we prioritise losing than winning)

comments.author: malsi_
comments.body:
To be clear, feel free to sign up with fake or throw away accounts, it doesn't matter   
a quick feed back is all i want 😄

comments.author: UnluckyBed2988
comments.body: Let me turn the costs up and see what happens to the curve I like moon spelling out its price bet fees and I would want that same clarity here with a way to try worse fill prices once you add slippage

replies.author: malsi_
replies.body:
adding custom fees is my next thing to ship   
as for slippage, tbh, i'm still hesitant on finding the correct way to impliment it 

i want to keep the backtesting process deterministic   
same strategy, same backtest params => same exact pnl to the cent 

introducing random slippage may effect AI raisoning (not sure yet) when it comes to detecting which config affected the results

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Keeping the backtest deterministic is a good call, and slippage doesn't need randomness to do that. Use a fixed cost per fill that depends on the bar, for example a share of the bar's range or a set number of basis points that widens when volatility is high. Then show results at a few preset levels (base and harsh) so users can see how fragile a result is. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source you could use to widen the cost automatically around news, where fills are worst.
